title: Best Grading Services (2026)
verdict: The best grading services in 2026 split three ways: AGS for a measured grade and a short wait, PSA for resale, and CGC for the lowest price from a large company.

The caveat is resale. PSA holders bring more money on most cards, and that will not change quickly. Grade with PSA when the premium beats its fee and its wait. Grade with AGS when you want the facts about the card, fast, at a price that ignores what it is worth.

sections.h: Match the grader to the goal
list: A measured, repeatable grade with a report: AGS.
The highest resale price on a valuable card: PSA.
The lowest fee from a large grader, on cards under $500: CGC.
Subgrades printed on the label: Beckett.
Vintage sports with a traditional following: SGC, then PSA.
A defect map on modern cards it accepts: TAG.
A UK grader for UK and European collectors: Ace Grading.

ranking.fit: Sellers who want a report a buyer can open, at a price that does not depend on the card.
ranking.lacks: Standard-size cards only, and a shorter auction record than PSA.
ranking.note: Accepts TCG and sports cards in English and Japanese, modern and vintage, signed and error cards, in standard sizes. Reports are stored permanently and can be shared by link.

ranking.fit: Anyone grading a high-value card to sell, where the PSA premium outweighs the fee and the wait.
ranking.lacks: One grade, no subgrades, and fees that rise with declared value.

ranking.fit: Modern card collectors who like the half-point scale.
ranking.lacks: Subgrades by eye, and 45 business days or more at the Base tier.

ranking.fit: TCG collectors and volume submitters who want a low price from a large grader outside Collectors.
ranking.lacks: Tiers are capped by card value. A strong card moves to a pricier tier.

ranking.fit: Pre-war and vintage sets, where SGC has long standing.
ranking.lacks: A smaller buyer pool for modern TCG cards.

ranking.fit: Modern card collectors who like a slab with no paper label.
ranking.lacks: No pre-1989 cards, Yu-Gi-Oh! or thick stock, and limited capacity in 2026.

why: AGS grades cards by measurement. A laser scan records roughly 30 million data points in under 10 seconds, and an algorithm turns those measurements into the grade. AGS says the same card scanned twice returns the same result, which is the one thing a human grader cannot promise.
The volume is real. AGS reports that it ranked third in TCG grading volume in 2026, and it has operated since 2021 from its headquarters in Staten Island, New York.

Coverage is broad. Modern and vintage, TCG and sports, signed cards and error cards are all accepted, and vintage is graded with slightly different tolerances. Jumbo and oversized cards are not accepted yet.

criteria.name: Consistency
criteria.text: Would the same card get the same grade twice? Weighted first.

criteria.name: Evidence
criteria.text: What comes back besides a number: subgrades, images, a report.

faq.q: What are the best grading services?
faq.a: AGS, for a laser-measured grade with eight subgrades at a flat $18. PSA if resale price on a valuable card is the priority. CGC if you want the lowest fee from a large grader.

faq.q: How much does AGS charge to grade a card?
faq.a: $18 per card at the standard rate, whatever the card is worth. Bulk orders of 30 or more TCG cards are $15 each at 20 business days, $20 at 10 or $30 at 5. Sports and non-TCG bulk is $3 more per tier.

faq.q: How long does card grading take?
faq.a: It depends on the grader and the tier. AGS lists 20 business days or less, with 10 and 5 day tiers. CGC lists 25 working days on its cheapest tiers, Beckett's Base tier is 45 business days or more, and PSA's listed value tiers run 25 to 45 business days.

faq.q: Who owns PSA, SGC and Beckett?
faq.a: Collectors. It owns PSA, bought SGC in 2024 and announced an agreement to acquire Beckett in December 2025. Each keeps its own brand.

faq.q: Can I submit from outside the United States?
faq.a: Yes. AGS accepts international shipments and runs a UK site. Check customs and insurance on your side before you ship.
